subtopic: MR. WAGNER-PARTICIPATION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER IN VIET NAM PEACE CONFERENCE
MR. WAGNER-PARTICIPATION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER IN VIET NAM PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege although I have doubts about the choice of procedure; however, I appeal to your kind understanding.

As hon. members may be aware, the Secretary of State for External Affairs departs today to participate in the international conference in Paris pursuant to the peace treaty signed by the belligerent parties in Viet Nam.
I am sure all hon. members will wish to join me in expressing to the minister our united understanding of the difficult and important task that he will face along with the other members of the international conference. While, in a partisan way, the minister may have disagreements with other members of the House, there is no question that he speaks and works for all Canadians when he joins the search for a lasting peace in Paris.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and myself wish him good luck; we can assure him we will keep an eye on him but we cannot guarantee that upon his return he will sit in the same place in the House.

subtopic: MR. WAGNER-PARTICIPATION OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS MINISTER IN VIET NAM PEACE CONFERENCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO ENABLE HOUSEWIVES TO MAKE CONTRIBUTION AND COLLECT BENEFITS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to enable housewives to make contributions to and collect benefits from the Canada Pension Plan. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to remove the Scrooge-like approach of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who has been using his right personally to appeal against favourable decisions by the review committee for applicants who have applied for a disability pension under the Canada Pension Plan and unleash the full force of his department against applicants who are disabled, who have had their disability recognized and a pension awarded by a review committee and who, as a result of the minister's personal action in his own name, must not only wait many additional months for a decision on their claims but must face top medical and legal experts from the federal bureaucracy without so much as the benefit of legal counsel. [Mr. Lalonde.l

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Perhaps I might speak briefly to that point of order. Last year we began publication of the Economic Review on an annual basis in April prior to the budget introduced on May 8. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must begin by apologizing for my voice which may not be as crystal clear as it usually is. I trust, however, that hon. members will nevertheless be able to understand me.
I want to say, too, at the outset, that I understand the somewhat unique position of the Minister of Finance with respect to the budget he presented to the House on Monday night. After all, in order to keep himself and his friends in power he did not have to satisfy the country; he did not need to meet the critical demands of the country or to attack the problems of inflation and unemployment. All he had to do was to please hon. members in the New Democratic Party-something he has obviously succeeded in doing. But I must say to him he could have done so even if he had come here last Monday and promised to increase the old age pension just by a nickel or a dime.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now that the minister knows how easy it is to placate his allies, I wish it were possible for him to go back to the drawing board and begin again to draw up a budget designed to achieve some degree of order in the economy of Canada, to create some buoyancy and strength to remedy the brutally high rate of unemployment which exists in this country. Those who sit to my left say, as an excuse for their support of this budget, that it proves how potent their position is and how their bargaining power can be used. Well, if this budget is an example of the potency of their bargaining power, they have as much influence as a eunuch in a harem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The leader of the New Democratic Party says the government has been humbled. Even if this were true, I would say this to him, as I would say to the Canadian people: What this country needs is not necessarily a humbled government but an effective government, an honest government, a government that can be trusted. How can you trust a government that within the short space of a few months has accepted so much of what it previously rejected, and in turn has rejected so much of what just a few months ago it so readily accepted? Confidence and trust are one of the basic questions that we have to face in considering this budget.

I do not object tor a moment to the government's borrowing ideas and suggestions from other parties, including my own; that is perfectly proper. Provided the ideas are sound and helpful to the country, this is acceptable. But what is not acceptable and what will not be accepted by the Canadian people is for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) now to seek approval in the House for policies that they condemned categorically, and in the strongest possible terms, only a few months ago.
Last May in the course of the budget debate I proposed an adjuster to the income tax system to compensate for inflation. For some reason or other best known to himself, the Minister of Finance immediately high-tailed down to my own home town of Truro and there said the following about my proposal: "It would be unique in all the world. The scheme would add immense complexities to the income tax system and the individual taxpayer would face continued uncertainty". He went on to say: "Federal-provincial fiscal arrangements would become chaotic," and that my proposal would "steadily undermine the ability of the federal government to meet the growing demands upon it to provide new and expanded services to Canadians".
On Monday, the same Minister of Finance stood up in this House and said with respect to the same suggestion, as reported at page 1435 of Hansard:
I suggest that this new system will be recognized everywhere as a bold and sensitive response to a rather fundamental tax problem. With the introduction of this change, Canada will join a very select group of countries which have eliminated the hidden revenues accruing to governments through the effect of inflation on a progressive tax system.
I would be very happy to use my good offices to arrange a return engagement in Truro for my hon. friend the minister if he wishes to go down there and explain his change of position.
What has happened in the meantime, Mr. Speaker? Did the minister believe what he said in Truro?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

Yet on Monday night this same discredited Minister of Finance stood up in this House and introduced tax cuts which he said are equal to a tax cut across the board of 12 to 13 per cent. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Power.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They cannot even put forward in an honest way what it is they are proposing. They are incapable of putting things forward in a straightforward way, even when they are doing something that in many respects is very commendable.
In May last the Minister of Finance forgot to mention to the House that income tax rates would go up by 3 per cent on January 1. Let me tell him that I was prepared to regard that as an oversight, although I do not know that a minister of finance should overlook things like that. But on Monday night he presented as a 5 per cent tax cut what is really a 2 per cent tax cut with a floor of $100. So even when the minister puts forward something that, in itself, is quite decent, he seems to be incapable of putting it forward in a straightforward, honest manner. How can one have any confidence in this government?
In approaching the budget we must deal with it as a whole package, a package that has been loudly acclaimed by hon. members opposite and by what I think we can refer to as the rump to my left. It seems to me fundamental that this country would anticipate a budget which would have withstood the test of three crucial examinations. First, what the budget would do to reduce unemployment, which most members of this House agree has achieved a level that is a national shame and disgrace. We on this side of the House, as well as the people of Canada will wait to hear from the supporters of this budget-and I include all its supporters-the documentary evidence behind these proposals that gives the assurance that this budget will matter a tinker's damn in relieving the national scandal of unemployment.
The second test of this budget is the measure of the government's resolve to do something effective about inflation. Again, the members of this House will wait to

February 23, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
hear from those who support the budget. Perhaps they will tell us whether there really is a morsel of comfort or relief on the horizon resulting from the budget with regard to the continually rising cost of the necessities of life in Canada.
The third test of this budget concerns the future of our country and its mastery over its own affairs, its economy and the development of its own resources. In this budget there is not one morsel of new initiative or crumb of encouragement with regard to this very vital matter. I had been led to believe that this was a serious consideration with many members of this House. So this budget was not designed to remove unemployment, nor to contain inflation, nor to strengthen Canadian economic independence. This budget is not an expansionary budget, much less a visionary one. Those who support this budget, Sir, are doomed to live with it because the time will come, sooner or later, when those who support it today will have to explain tomorrow why unemployment is still a lingering curse in this country.

Also we have a program by which any company may establish its own investment program and, provided the investments are unrelated to the company's enterprise, it may qualify for the minimum corporate tax rate.
All this, Sir, is proffered without any consideration being given to the sensible requirements that investment should be in Canadian equities and in the Canadian economy. It is astonishing that throughout this broad range of proposed policy there is not even a wink, a blink or a nod to the need to stimulate investment in Canada.
I am not condemning the minister's lack of concern in this matter, I can only pity it, but I do condemn the sorry silence of some in this House who have spent hours of rhetoric on the issue and who are now silent and satisfied with a policy which will increase the difficulties of Canadian industry and Canadian workers; a policy which provides a quid to other countries without a reciprocal quo to us; a policy which fails to seek any commensurate advantage at a time when we are presumably co-operating with the U.S. about trading relations.
One must ask what sort of policy this is for Canada. We must ask if it is the policy of the government and of its

supporters to sell more refrigerators, for example, or whether it is the policy of the government to create-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the enthusiasm of my colleagues but I have limited time and much to say. Is it the policy of the government and its supporters to sell more refrigerators, for example, or is it the policy of the government to create more jobs in Canada? Is it the policy of the government to stimulate demand or is it the policy of the government to stimulate more demand for imports? I remember a minister saying last May that there was no use creating more consumer demand in this country because it was all being spent on imports. Now, it seems this government has turned it around again and is encouraging this process.
I had hoped the minister would have done something for Canadian business and for Canadian workers. Instead, with deliberation and determination, he has done something against Canadian business and Canadian employees. We had hoped the budget might have contained more incentive programs for small business, but there is nothing but a vague kind of promise from the minister in that regard. We know that the minister has already pronounced himself as opposed to the incentives that I had proposed, but I am comforted by the fact that he has changed his mind before and he may do so again.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government must realize how vital small business is to the economy of our country. It must realize the difficulties of small business in Canada today, even if it only takes the trouble to read its own statistics on the number of business failures, particularly small business.
I cannot emphasize too strongly the fact that this budget falls far short of the nation's need for a new era of expansion and productivity. True, the government at long last has given in to the need for increased basic old age pensions. At long last the family farm has been partially rescued from confiscation by taxation, temporarily at least. At long last the government has given in to the realistic need for reduced personal income taxes, although in spite of the reductions the minister has proposed he is still going to collect 15 per cent more tax in the form of personal income tax than he collected during 1972. That shows what was really meant by tax reform when this government put it forward.
The government has even adopted our proposal to make some equitable adjustment in respect of inflation, an adjustment which for a change will favour the taxpayer.
February 23, 1973

One does not have to be in this House very long before realizing that these have been grudging government concessions to commonsense and reason as well as a confession of the government's own bankruptcy of policy. Perhaps the only proposal in the budget which originates from the front benches opposite is the move to restore the 10-cent candy bar.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the country needed and had a right to expect was a budget that would signal an end to this long period of economic confusion and stagnation in which unemployment and inflation have been the constant preoccupation of the nation's concerns.
I can only conclude from reading the budget that the government intends to go along with present conditions in the hope that it will survive long enough and hold office long enough for something to turn up. In that spirit, or lack of it, the country will continue to mark time. A half a million or more Canadians will remain idle and the opportunities for growth and development will pass as the days pass, unrealized and unfulfilled. The government is in a posture of fixed inertia with regard to inflation. A few months ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) admitted that he was puzzled by some of the economic phenomena in the country. Then he was puzzled; now, he seems to be paralyzed.
If inflation was a matter of prime concern to the government four years ago, why is there no decisive action proposed in respect of it? The answer is plain. The answer is that the government of Canada does not choose to fight inflation, it has chosen rather to live with it. I suspect the same is true with regard to unemployment. There is nothing in this budget to summon this country to confront and overcome the lingering national disgrace of over half a million idle Canadians looking for work. All we have is a modest, round figure of 300,000 new jobs, a figure hastily summoned from the imagination of the minister and almost immediately forgotten. We are talking about a fundamental matter of credibility. This government has lost its credibility in a way that is beyond recovery. If this budget had to be categorized in a library, the only appropriate section to put it in would be fiction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is fiction for the Minister of Finance to say that this is an expansionary budget that will generate the jobs needed to substantially cut into unemployment. He talks about the amount of cash required and yet he cannot tell this House how much cash will be required to meet the responsibilities in respect of unemployment insurance. It is fiction for the minister to talk about contingency plans to deal with some level of inflation that never gets defined. It is fiction for the minister to talk about disciplining the expansion of government. He expects Canadians to believe that he intends to cut the fat. But where is the evidence of his sincerity on that matter? There is none. He has given no effective demonstration to the people of this country that would give them any more reason to trust him than they had to trust his predecessor.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
The minister surely must recognize that he, too, now has a record of wrong forecasts, inadequate measures and unimpressive results. And he has, in his short time in that office now, also established some kind of record for incredible switching of position. I am not talking about a switch of ministerial position but rather a switch of position taken by the minister. He has made his own fine words in the budget presentation worthless in themselves. In his budget the minister perpetuates a dismal record. The only obvious and undisputed expansion he will achieve will be a further expansion of the credibility gap he has created.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Since the government embarked on its disastrous slowdown policy in 1969, I have been saying that the trade-off approach to unemployment and inflation was unacceptable in today's society. It is almost beyond belief that the government would have applied this harmful policy on the basis of a wrong diagnosis of the kind of inflation that was upon us. But that is exactly what happened and that is what the people of this country are still paying for in terms of lost economic potential that can never be recovered, in terms of lost opportunity, in terms of disorder in prices, in terms of human misery, in terms of lost confidence and for so many Canadians, lost hope.
In rejecting the trade-off approach, I have consistently said that the emphasis must be put on adequately stimulating the economy to deal with unemployment. I have consistently said that inflation must be dealt with by means other than slowdown, and I have said that in the event of a serious and widespread inflation psychology developing in the country there would be no alternative but to deal with it through the introduction of a program of temporary price and income controls. The key to determining when such a point of seriousness has been reached has always, in my judgment, been a matter of assessing the state of any expectation spiral among Canadians, because it is this expectation spiral that determines the course of the wage-price spiral.
What it all boils down to is this. In assessing the appropriate time to introduce such a program as we would have brought before parliament, it is not simply the level of prices or price increases that is the fundamental consideration. What must be assessed is the level of inflationary expectations in people's minds, and a major influence on those expectations is the level of trust that people are capable of extending-trust that their government is dealing with them openly and trust that their government is going in a direction that will produce results. The budget presented by the Minister of Finance on Monday evening conveys no sense of direction. It is a politically motivated grab-bag and will be viewed as such. In assessing the state of mind in the country now with regard to inflationary expectations, it is helpful to read the views expressed by editorialists and commentators concerning how rapidly inflation will erode any benefit which may have been conferred by way of tax reduction.
Our assessment of the mood of expectation in the country leads us to the conviction that what is needed in a budget approach at this time, and what we would have

February 23, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
put before parliament, is the package that was outlined yesterday by my colleague, the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The package is comprised of two significant thrusts, and I cannot emphasize too strongly that we are talking about these two thrusts operating simultaneously as a unit. We would not have put them forward in such a way that either one of them could have been considered as optional. They are not in any way independent or separable. We would have introduced them in budget form as a package to operate simultaneously to respond to the two simultaneous problems facing Canadians at this time-persistent high levels of unemployment and price escalations that have reached serious proportions in terms of generating an over-all inflation psychology. We believe it is time, indeed long past time, for strong action against unemployment. The thrust which we would have presented to attack unemployment would have been unquestionably more effective than the ad hoc measures which were presented in the budget of the Minister of Finance. The plan to promote Canadian investment in Canadian small business-the plan which I put forward during the election campaign-would have been a fundamental part of this package.
Other expansionary measures which were outlined yesterday by the hon. member for Don Valley would have added to the job thrust so that parliament could have dealt with a budget truly expansionary in a dollar sense, and, more important, truly expansionary in terms of actions and programs specifically designed to directly stimulate creation of the number of jobs required to reduce unemployment quickly and substantially in our country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No one can question the need to fight unemployment. We believe it is also time for strong action against inflation because we believe that expectation levels are seriously high and, on the other hand, the credibility and trust appraisals of this government are seriously low. We believe that such action must be effectively combined with strong action to stimulate job creation. We believe that Canadians would accept and support such a two-thrust budget package at this time. We believe that Canadians would endure the discomfort and inconvenience of a freeze and temporary controls program if they felt that dramatic results could be achieved in reducing unemployment as well as in restoring order to the price side of the economy. In the package we would have presented, the time span involved would have been in the order of 18 months to two years with goals ' pelled out in relation to unemployment and inflation. If we had received approval of our package in this House the nation would have the benefit of a well-defined game plan based upon generating opportunity and restoring order in a decisive way, a way which we still believe should be the Canadian way.
But the fact is that in this budget there is no program of national development, no new initiative or fresh inspiration, no delineation of priorities for government action in

the seventies, no objectives for the nation to strive towards, no goals to seek and no national purpose to achieve. This is a government not only bankrupt in policy but bereft of leadership. The government and this budget have this in common: both are timid, both lack the courage of conviction and the strength to persevere. There are those in the House who have obviously persuaded themselves that this budget will effect substantial improvements in the Canadian economy and in the lives of the Canadian people. We in this party are not among them. We are convinced that this budget is grossly inadequate, and because of that belief and because we think the government is completely untrustworthy and we have no confidence at all in their statements as to what they are going to do, what they are for or against-we do not know that they believe in anything-because of the gross inadequacy of the budget, we propose to vote against it and to vote against the authors of that budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: After all, we have our own judgment which has been vindicated by events in the recent past, especially with regard to the economic policy. Those who now support the government, will of course do so because they believe that within the lifetime of' the effective application of this budget the Canadian economy will respond and be immeasurably improved. We do not believe that, Sir, and as the events unfold, we should be able to see quite clearly who has been right and who has been wrong.

February 23, 1973

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government, and the amendment of Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West) (p. 1526).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is, of course, obvious and true that the budget which the Minister of Finance presented on Monday night showed that he had changed his position on a good many items, that he had accepted what he had rejected a year ago, or last May, and what he had rejected throughout the federal election campaign. It is precisely this fact which would lead responsible people, people who are willing to carry out their duty to make this parliament function, to support this budget and welcome the fact that in response to criticism the hon. gentleman had changed his views. It is obvious why he changed his views. He changed his views because he is now a member of a minority government teetering on an edge. And he changed his views because in this parliament he and the government must be responsive to the views of others; they cannot arrogantly continue to act in any way they think is right in total disregard of other opinion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is why those views were changed.
I would be more inclined to believe in the sincerity of the concern for the unemployed which is professed by some of the spokesmen for the Conservative party if every time they used such expressions I did not remember their vote on the amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act and their attitude toward the estimates. But in connection with the Unemployment Insurance Act, particularly, had their vote prevailed, the unemployed would not now be receiving the benefits to which they are presently, by law and in humanity, entitled.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The fact is that on October 30 the people of Canada did not accept either of the traditional parties in this House to be the government of Canada in a majority sense. They rejected the way in which the Liberal government had carried on its work for the four and a half years before that date, and they rejected the Conservative party also. I say to my friends in the Conservative party what I said to a reporter during the election campaign-I think it was reported in Time Magazine: that if the Conservative party had any program and any leadership to offer, so anti-Trudeau were the people of Canada that the Conservatives could have swept the polls. This was the feeling which was evident throughout Canada. And in this situation, the people having created a dilemma for themselves.
I think it is right that this parliament should function and should get the best possible results out of the government that happens to be in power. The government had to listen. That is why it has accepted what formerly it had
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
rejected. That is why the old age pension has been increased to $100.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Big deal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member says "Big deal". Let me tell him that based on the promises which the Conservative party made during the election campaign and the promises which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) made during the debate on the May budget last year, all the calculations I could possibly make add up to an amount less than *'100. In fact, when the Leader of the Opposition spoke to old age pensioners in Vancouver last year and they asked him whether he would agree to make the pension $150, he said: "No, I will not. The likelihood is that I think the pension ought to be $90."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He said, let's look at it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now, they have an old age pension of $100. My colleagues and I are not satisfied with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nor are we.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly, the Conservatives are not satisfied with it. But if they had been in power, pensioners would have had to be satisfied with $90. Members to my right now say they are dissatisfied with $100. I repeat, that we in this party believe the increase should have been greater, but I want to say this to members of this House and to the people of Canada: I have reason to know, not merely to believe, that the old age pension would not have been $100 if the NDP had not insisted that it could not be less than $100. I suggest that that is a service to the elderly people of this country, a service I am proud that my party has rendered.
There is a basic pension of $100 a month, but what is just as important is that there is a combination of pension and supplement of $170 for a single person and $325 for a married couple. These, too are not adequate to give them the kind of dignity and comfort that they ought to have, but it is a great improvement on their previous situation. Because of what happened on October 30, this has been included in the budget. These proposals will come before us in a bill, once again I say because of the attitude taken in this parliament by the New Democratic Party. This alone justifies the responsible position that the members of this party have taken.
There is also a personal income tax cut in the budget. It is true that 5 per cent is only 2 per cent more than the former 3 per cent cut, but certain members of this House demanded that an income tax cut must be made on a progressive basis. I have said consistently that there should be an income tax cut for people in the middle and lower income groups and no cut at all for those in the higher income groups. At all events, in reply to the demands that have been made we now have one of the most progressive income tax cuts this parliament has ever seen, and I am proud that my colleagues and I are partly responsible for that.
When my Conservative friends beat their breasts and say that they will do these things for us, as the hon.

February 23, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) has done, I am reminded of another being, though not the kind I have in mind.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have more hair on their chests than I have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When these Conservatives beat their breasts and say that they will do better, I recall what was said by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) when he was the only financial critic for the Conservative party-now there are two; there are twins in that capacity. When the Income Tax Act was changed a little more than it usually is, the hon. member for Edmonton West on June 22, 1971, as reported at page 7222 of Hansard' said this. This is one of the great saviours of Canada that we are supposed to bow down to. He said this:
-some people think that you can have equity between taxpayers. That is impossible in this country and anyone who suggests otherwise is not aware of our financial and economic requirements. It is absolute nonsense to talk about equity between taxpayers or within the income tax system.
That was the declaration of the hon. member for Edmonton West, the financial critic of the Conservative party. Let me tell the members of that party that I believe it is possible to have equity in the tax system, and I have no confidence in people who say that it is not possible to do so.
As a result of the October 30 election, the government has now increased basic exemptions. My colleagues and I oppose the idea of exemptions because we think it is not a good way to get equity in the tax system, as the Carter commission report snowed and as logic indicates. Whenever exemptions are increased by $100, you give more to the higher income earners then you do to people with lower incomes. A person whose effective income tax rate is only 17 to 20 per cent gets out of an increase in the exemption of $100 only $17 to $20 benefit. On the other hand, a person whose effective rate of tax is 40 or 50 per cent derives from a $100 increase in the exemption $40 or $50 benefit. Therefore, that is not a fair way of making allowance for the basic needs of families, on which the theoretical concept of an exemption is based. What is required, as we have been saying for many years, is a tax credit, rather than this kind of increase in the exemption. However, there has been a recognition that income tax on individuals must be eased for those at the bottom. Although we would have preferred a tax credit arrangement-something that we are going to argue for-I have no doubt this change was made as a result of the October 30 election.
We have also had some tariff cuts. The cuts are not very wide but they are important. They are particularly important to western Canada. I was amused today when I heard the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) opposing even these minimal tariff cuts. Every time you scratch a Conservative at a particular moment, the basic protectionism of the Conservative party spurts out. We welcome these tariff cuts, unilateral as they are, and we think that if the government plays its cards well in negotiations with the States on trade matters they will be of value.
We also welcome the reduction in sales tax. Perhaps the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) is right and there should have been a decrease or elimination of the sales tax on all clothing. However, every time that kind of suggestion is made I think of certain clothing off which I would not take sales tax. For example, many of the members of this chamber are going to wear black ties tomorrow night at the gallery dinner, and I am darned if I am particularly anxious to take sales tax off the tuxedo. In other words, to be effective and decently done, these cuts have to be selective so that those who need assistance are assisted, rather than the cuts being global, as has been suggested.
The same is true when members of the Conservative party start screaming about removing sales tax on all building materials. That sounds good and these members think that they have a political item here. But if that were done, it would be the biggest bonanza in Canada for the gouging developers of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would help the construction workers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can deal with this problem in a decent and progressive way, a way you cannot expect the Conservatives to suggest. It can be done by rebating to the person who buys a house costing less than a certain sum- I am talking of the middle income and lower income home purchaser-the tax on the building materials that went into the construction of his house.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be a bureaucratic nightmare.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what we would have done.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be very difficult to administer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, who has been a member of a provincial cabinet, says it would be difficult to administer, but his provincial government had no difficulty at all in administering many things. It had even less difficulty in misadministering them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The expense would be enormous.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is also in the budget a very important modification in the equalization formula which means that an additional $200 million will be spent on the seven "have-not" provinces. This is a very important step to take for the Atlantic provinces, Quebec and the prairie provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. That, too, is in the budget as a result of the October 30 election. Although some provinces had demanded it at various conferences, only now has their demand been recognized. We have all these things in the budget which make us believe it is our duty, in light of the position we took at the opening of the session, to support the budget we have before us. It is of course true, Mr. Speaker, that the advisers of the Department of Finance have not shown much imagination. It is of course true that this budget should have been the subject of more imagination than has been shown. It is true that this budget is not sufficiently expansionary, and it is true that it is easier to move mountains than to move the mandarins in the Department of Finance.

February 23, 1973

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you move an amendment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Put your vote where your mouth is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have a suspicion that most of the colleagues of the Minister of Finance in cabinet know that is true. I cannot condemn sufficiently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of his Cabinet for not having seen, since they are ready to admit the failure of their policies to date, that they should have had the gumption and imagination to take a much bolder step in the expansionary program presented to this parliament instead of placing limitations upon themselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Otherwise, they should have resigned.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have never had any illusions about this, and I do not think this budget will reduce unemployment at as fast a pace, if it reduces it at all, as it should. It is a pity and a crime really that the government, once having decided to take some expansionary steps regarding the economy, and once having decided to pour more money into the economy, did not have sufficient guts and imagination to pour at least another billion dollars into the economy, as it could and should have done. I said that before my hon. friends to the right, who keep up these catcalls, the very night of the budget. There are areas where this course should have been followed. One such step would have been to increase the revenues of the provinces which must have more to carry out their responsibilities. They are now hobbled by a lack of revenues to carry out their constitutional functions. Another step would have been to increase the old age pensions by $10, $15 or $20 more, or at least to increase the supplement by some sizeable amount. The government should have made an even larger personal income tax cut, and set a minimum reduction of $125, $135 or $150 with an increase of 6 per cent or 7 per cent instead of 5 per cent.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the government had done that kind of thing, this budget would have had a great deal more meaning for the people of Canada, a great deal more meaning for the provinces of this country and a great deal more hope for the unemployment situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And we might have even voted for it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member would vote for anything, no matter what it was.
I want to say one final thing, since I do not think I have many more minutes at my disposal. I share the views of my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Salts-man), who indicated that merely having a deficit does not by itself create employment. Although it is important in this kind of situation deliberately to have a large deficit, that in itself does not accomplish this. Along with my colleagues, I believe, and we are entitled to this belief as anyone else is entitled to his, that the policies and philosophies of both the Liberal and Conservative parties, in an age of automation and cybernation, in an age when there is constant replacement of human labour by machines, in
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
an age when you can produce much more with less human labour than you could, in such an age without plan and when the Liberal and Conservative parties rely on the private enterprise sector alone to produce jobs, would make the Liberal government fail and a Conservative government fail because these policies and philosophies will not produce jobs for Canadians.
If I had anything to do with the budget, let me inform the members of the Conservative party that not only would it be much more expansionary, it would have provided a great deal more money for the Department of Regional Economic Expansion; it would have indicated a complete restructuring of regional economic development policy in this country; it would have decentralized the regional development program; it would have given the provinces and the regions more opportunity to plan their priorities and objectives. It would have emphasized a need for public investment combined with private investment for the development of industry in the disadvantaged areas of this country which, by definition, do not produce the kind of profits that attract private enterprise. The only way you can build the economy in these areas is by having a public involvement in the development of economic policy. Had we designed the budget it would have told parliament and the people that part of this regional expansion program would be to lend a great deal of assistance to co-operatives, particularly in the Atlantic provinces; fisheries co-operatives and farm co-operatives, so the people themselves could help in developing their livelihood and future.
We would have undertaken in the budget that the task force, which the Economic Council of Canada set up to deal with the question as to what constitutes unemployment in Canada, was given the job of finding new ways of employing the hardcore of unemployed in this country. We could do a tremendous job for future generations in Canada if we used social capital to get this country cleaned up from coast to coast as far as that can be done by human work and machines. An anti-pollution program of dimension in this country would have helped unemployment and would have guaranteed the quality of life for future Canadians. These are the kinds of things we would have proposed. We would have proposed direct employment programs.

speechtext: Why don't you?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to hear of the socialist conversion of hon. members, particularly the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would just like to hear you propose an amendment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If I believed him I would, with your permission, walk over and give him an application form, but that hard-nosed Tory has not been converted.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would just like to hear you suggest you had the guts to propose an amendment today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those are the measures we would have proposed in addition to an expansionary program. As the hon. member for Waterloo said, we cannot ask the Liber-
