als or Conservatives to accept, adopt and implement a New Democratic Party policy because that is not what we would expect them to do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why don't you try an amendment?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I told those hon. gentlemen in Toronto the other day that I was certain they would vote for the communist manifesto if they thought they could get across the aisle and become the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Give us the chance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have no doubt they would vote for any amendment put forward, without caring what it said, as long as they thought the amendment would carry. Because I do not expect this government or any other government of another party to bring our program forward, I feel and my colleagues feel it our duty to support this budget and to be proud that our presence here has produced many more things for the people of Canada than would otherwise have been the case.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a very interesting day, at least up until now. We heard the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) tell us all that is wrong in Canada. To use the words of the Leader of the Opposition, he said there is nothing but confusion and stagnation in Canada. The Leader of the New Democratic Party told us there is much wrong. If there were people from other countries of the world such as Germany, France, Russia, England or the United States sitting in the gallery today, they would think that perhaps this is the worst country in the world. I say it is high time that as Members of Parliament we started telling the world what is good about Canada, and started sticking up for Canada for a change. Much is wrong, of course, with Canada. It is not any Heaven, but it is still the best country in the whole world with one of the highest standards of living, with the best housing and where we have a policy of looking after our senior citizens better than they are looked after in any other country in the world. I could go on and on in this vein.
It was interesting to hear the Leader of the Opposition this morning tell us what is wrong. It was also interesting to hear the Leader of the New Democratic Party in his most efficient manner tell us why he would support us over here instead of those horrible people to the right of him. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, why he supports us. He supports us because he is afraid to do anything else. I am the fellow who will tell him right now that he is afraid, as are the people behind him. He told us today, and on numerous other occasions, that he does not like us any more than the people to his right. So, the answer is that what all the people behind him are thinking about is their seats, particularly those from western Canada. They do not want an election in the near future. In the light of what the two leaders of the parties said this morning and

again this afternoon, it was obvious they certainly were not sticking up for each other.
May I say I listened to the lead-off speaker for the Conservative party, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and also listened attentively to his lieutenant, the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) yesterday afternoon, but I did not find any similarity in their speeches. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Edmonton West said that his amendment was being moved because this budget would not reduce either unemployment or inflation or the spiralling cost of living. I did not hear the hon. member for Don Valley speak very much about that. The main theme of his speech centred around the fact that if the conservatives had the opportunity they would place a 90-day freeze on wages, salaries, prices and so on. The hon. member for Edmonton West who led off and moved the amendment did not even mention the possibility of a wage or price freeze in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, he did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As has been suggested, perhaps our Tory friends should hold a caucus meeting next Wednesday morning to decide what their position is in respect of budget, because evidently they are not all telling the same story.
Inasmuch as I do not have the same length of time as some other hon. members, may I ask that members take the time to read some of the highlights in the budget and then go home where, in the quietness of their own rooms, they can say they are really proud they are still Canadians and have the responsibility and obligation to pay taxes in this fine land. Let us look, for example, at the first item. The basic exemption for all taxpayers has been increased from $1500 to $1600. Perhaps this might seem to be of little significance, but the point is that the basic exemption was the highest in the world before last Monday night and now is even higher. This is something of which Canadians can be proud.
Not only has the basic exemption been increased to $1600 from $1500, but let us see what has been done for the senior citizens. Their exemption at age 65 will not be $1600 but rather $2600. This is the highest exemption in respect of senior citizens anywhere in the world. My hon. friends did not mention that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not enough.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the story we hear all the way through-too late and not enough. I say to some of the people across the way who want the responsibility to govern that you cannot give everything away without increasing taxes. For the last several weeks we, and my friends on the other side of the House, have been talking about the old age pension situation. No one appreciates more than I do the fact that our senior citizens need assistance, but what has not been said is that the old age pension scheme before last Monday night in Canada was the best in the whole world. They did not say that the basic exemption for our senior citizens is the highest in the world, or that at age 65 in most provinces senior citizens receive free hospitalization and medicare in Canada. They did not mention the other things such as
February 23, 1973

cheaper housing and rentals. One must take everything in context and not try to dwell on one point. The fact is that our senior citizens know they are not getting too much, but they do know that they are getting more than the senior citizens in the United States, in France, in England, in Russia or anywhere else in the world.
Not just the people in the Liberal party but also those in the Conservative party and New Democratic Party should be very proud of the way in which we are attempting to look after our senior citizens. I did not hear my friends mention anything about the increases which are to be given to the recipients of the war veterans allowance. I did not hear my hon. friends mention the fact that we still have over one million veterans in Canada out of a total of 22 million people. Those who are in receipt of war veterans allowance will find that the allowance for married recipients has been increased to $357 a month. Once again, I say we should be very proud of that. I could go on and on. I did not hear my hon. friend from Don Valley say anything about the fact that it will now be possible to pass family farms on from generation to generation free of a capital gains tax.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is a great idea. I only had 30 minutes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I heard hon. members opposite say that other small businesses should be allowed to pass to the next generation free of a capital gains tax, but I did not hear them give any credit for what has been done. I did not hear any credit being given for the fact that, for the first time since the war years, the agriculture industry in Canada is starting to receive a fair deal. More grain is being sold now, and at higher prices, than has been the case for many years. So far as the agriculture industry is concerned the light of day is now being seen in respect of many products for the first time, but my Tory or NDP friends did not mention this. I could carry on and mention many other things. Let us think about some of the other good things we have in Canada. Let us stand up for Canada.
We have one of the finest educational systems in the whole world, one of the finest hospitalization systems in the world. They are not perfect by any means. However, if you think we have poor housing in the city of Toronto- there is none in Don Valley-go to Harlem in New York city and take a look at really poor housing, and that is the wealthiest city in the whole world. We are not perfect in Canada, but we have the very best there is. Ask our friends who are in the Caribbean: why is it that more Canadians travel than do the people of any other country in the world?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are on LIP grants.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The answer is, because we are more prosperous.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are on Opportunities for Youth grants.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not mind interruptions from the other side, but I hope you understand I only have a few
The Budget-Mr. Whicher
minutes because I am a back-bencher. I do not, therefore have many opportunities to speak.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would not take too long to cut you down to size. You will be a lot smaller, my friend.
Why is it that these good things are taking place in Canada? I will say this: the reason that we have these good things is our high standard of living. This country is not perfect by any means, as I said. The reason we have these good things is that over many years we have had an excellent democratic government here in Canada, and the one that we have at present is no exception.
I heard the speech of my friend, the hon. member for Don Valley whom I appreciate very much and I think he gave a wonderful speech yesterday. Let me say, incidentally, that he comes from the riding of Bruce. However, I was amused when I heard him say that one of the things the Conservatives would do, if they had funds, would be to reduce the age at which the old age pension is granted from 65 to 64. This is a wonderful promise but I cannot help but feel that the last time my Conservative friends had the opportunity to raise old age pensions they raised them from $55 to $65, and not at the age of 65 but at the age of 70.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Poor comparison.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These are facts, my friend. You should go back to your colleagues and start learning some of these things. I do not know what these fellows are, but they are confused, I will tell you that.
These are the things that we must think about here in Canada. We have many problems. There is not any one on this side of the House who is proud of the fact that we have 6 i per cent unemployment, but in remembering that fact let us face the reality that some of those people for various reasons, do not want to work. They may be semiretired or may have other reasons. But let us remember that if we have 6J per cent unemployment, it means that 93 J per cent in Canada are working. We should not forget that. When the hon. member for Don Valley suggests we should bring unemployment down to 5J per cent, as our American friends have done, let us not forget that for the past number of years they have been fighting one off the worst wars in history with three million men under arms and with armies all over the world. Perhaps if we wanted to have an army on that scale we might bring our unemployment down to 5 i per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is absurd.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On the other hand, there is no doubt that the unemployment situation in Canada must be remedied. Everyone on this side of the House says so. As a matter of fact, the very first thing that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) recommended in his budget speech the other night was to lower unemployment figures in Canada and to lessen inflation. After all, we are controlled to a large extent, so far as inflation is concerned, by the outside world. We have a country to the south of us with ten times our population and 15 times our gross national product. If General Motors workers in Detroit ask for wage
1608

February 23, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Frank
increases, I suggest that General Motors workers in Oshawa or Windsor will ask for similar increases. We are tied to the U.S. rate of inflation. But my friends on the other side, of course, are not tied to anything. They are in a position of being able to criticize and they take advantage of this at every opportunity.
In conclusion I want to say to hon. members: do not sell this country of ours short. It has never been sold in that way in the past. I say, as I did when I started, that it is high time, while we recognize the fact that we have many problems in Canada, the problems were ploughed under by the good things that have been accomplished over the years and are continuing to be done even unto this day.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a great honour and privilege to have the opportunity to enter into this budget debate, particularly at the early stages, and to speak on the same day as our leader.
First of all, I wish to extend my congratulations to you, and they are just as sincere now as they were at the beginning. As a matter of fact, over these several weeks, both you and the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), have given me ample opportunity to appreciate the very impartial and objective approach which you exemplify and which has been so evident throughout the proceedings of this House. I am sure that each new member, as he attempts to adjust to this new and challenging environment, forms many different opinions of parliament and its members. Let me assure you, even though I have always had a high opinion of this institution, it has certainly been heightened further and you, Mr. Speaker, have indeed contributed to this.
Before I get into the serious part of my speech as it relates to the budget, I would like to take the opportunity provided by a maiden speech to expound on the many virtues of the riding which I am both proud and humble to represent, namely, Middlesex. Actually, considering the geographic area which this riding encompasses, it should be called London Middlesex Lambton. About one third of the electorate of my riding lives in that great city of London which is conveniently situated midway between Windsor and Toronto and which has a population of well over 200,000. The balance is made up of most of the county of Middlesex which encircles London, plus a portion of the county of Lambton. This, in itself, makes the riding unique in many ways.
I should like to deal first of all with some of the factors that make the city of London so important, not only the portion of that city in my riding but in total. The London area has long been recognized as a very important education centre, having that great University of Western Ontario in its midst. This university has been noted, not only for its many distinguished graduates, but also for its growth, never more so than in these recent years when many new buildings have been added to the university campus, such as the new D. B. Weldon library, the extended cancer research area, the new faculty of dentistry, and the new university community centre which, incidentally, was a $4.5 million project with the students paying roughly $140,000 a year over a 20 year period. In the fall of 1972, a new university hospital was opened adjacent to the campus, and more buildings will be put up. There are, of course, many affiliated colleges surrounding the campus,
[Mr. Whicher.l
such as the London Teachers College, and the Althouse Secondary Teachers College. We can also boast of the Fanshaw College of Applied Arts and Sciences, a new college with a full time enrolment of some 3,300 students.
London is proud of its many financial institutions, being the home of several head offices. These are made up of insurance companies, trust companies, and a very pleasant and necessary mixture of industry, both large and small. Although all of these important institutions and areas are not necessarily situated within the city boundaries of my riding, my constituents certainly share the responsibility and, I believe, some of the credit for their existence.
My riding has many towns and villages spotted here and there among the farms. The largest of these towns is Strathroy, with a population of close to 7,000. Middlesex riding rates second in terms of acreage of improved farmland in Ontario with some 538,013 acres. It has been long recognized as the home of many prominent breeders of Holstein dairy cattle, having the second highest production of No. 1 milk in Ontario with 142,700,000 pounds, and also of Aberdeen Angus and Hereford cattle. We certainly have our share of swine breeders and sheep breeders. We can also boast of some of the finest horses, a number of which have been recognized in many of the great horse shows in North America.
My riding is well recognized in the poultry industry, being the home of the largest turkey hatchery not only in North America but in the world. This hatchery supplies a large percentage of the Canadian market, as well as the United States, with turkey poults, and this year will ship close to one million eggs to Europe, opening up yet another vast area of exports. My riding can also be credited with the highest hen laying population in Ontario, and probably in all of Canada.
Crop production is still another area in which we need not take a back seat, although corn would be by far the greatest acreage, placing second in Ontario with 130,531 acres, and I share with my colleague from Huron the only Canadian-owned seed-corn production company in Canada, Stuarts Hybreds. We produce large quantities of beans, placing second in Ontario in white bean production, plus of course general cereal crops. And provided that the government can come up with a Canadian sugar policy, Mr. Speaker, you will also see production of sugar beets in my area for the proposed plant in southwestern Ontario.
These products I briefly mention are only the basis of a far more encompassing production pattern as the result of cross-breeding, which in turn produces volume that has only scratched the surface of what can be done, if the agricultural community has the confidence in the future that it must have for it to do any long-range planning.
All these things in my riding did not just happen. It has taken the efforts of responsible citizens at all levels of society, whether they be union or non-union employees, large or small employers, large or small businesses-both urban and rural-and large or small farms. They have all exhibited a responsibility to the steady growth of a city
February 23, 1973

and surrounding area that is the true symbol of a free enterprise system.
If these citizens of the city of London and the surrounding rural areas are going to continue to progress in the manner that they have in the past and, Mr. Speaker, they are no different from millions of other citizens throughout this great Canada of ours, they must have confidence in a federal government leadership that will give them the incentive that they so desperately need. This, Mr. Speaker, is the background for a few areas that I would like to elaborate on this afternoon. Canadians have the right to expect positive leadership, from their federal government, and not just a group of followers.
To illustrate what I mean, Mr. Speaker, I think we have had the greatest exhibition of kite flying that this country has ever known, during what will be known in history as the Trudeau years. Now, when I mention kite flying I do not mean the recent exhibition on the front lawn of parliament a few weeks ago. I am referring to the time the former Minister of Finance subjected this country to that monstrosity known as the white paper on taxation. I was not a member at that time. I was one of the hundreds of thousands of employers, owner of a small business in particular, who frantically enlisted every means possible to try and convince the then minister of the folly of such legislation as it related to small business.
Mr. Speaker, such kite flying cost this country untold hundreds of thousands of dollars in accountants' and lawyers' fees, and after many months of frustration and expensive anxiety we were informed that the 50 per cent taxation on all business, large or small, would not be implemented as proposed. There were also concessions in other areas, but the point of it all is that when this same Prime Minister and his supercircle of advisers finally realized this tax paper was not acceptable, they simply passed it off with another shrug and said, "We never intended to implement it; we just wanted to see what the people thought about it".
That was my impression of the government of the day, looking in from the outside. Now that I am here, I am sorry to say we seem to be saddled with the same idea of following. Mr. Speaker, the proof of all this was once again displayed by yet another Minister of Finance last Monday evening when he attempted to convince the taxpayers of the soundness of an original tax plan, when in fact he was capitalizing on one of the Leader of the Opposition's (Mr. Stanfield) own sound proposals in the last campaign.
Small business must have more reasonable assurances of stability in the future, or Canadian small business failures will continue to rise, even at a greater rate than in 1972, which was the highest period. The free enterprise system that encourages individuals to launch their own ideas and optimism, through outlets of their own small businesses, is still alive, even after such negative federal discouragement these past few years, and more particularly from this last budget. The small business concession in this budget does nothing for the man who wants to start up, or is already in production but cannot find reasonable capital to continue. Such people are the embryo of unlimited employment potential if given a chance. But financial institutions today are not interested in taking that
The Budget-Mr. Frank
chance, so I feel it is up to the federal government to provide the necessary confidence.
I know of the frustration of small business. I had the nerve to start one in 1956, with no excess capital but with lots of enthusiasm and energy. It is an agri-business, so you know it was never lucrative to the lending institutions, government or otherwise. But today, from a one-man and my family beginning, this business now maintains over 25 employees, and distributes brand name products, two of them with my own Canadian and United States patents, to all provinces across Canada and much of the United States, and with even a shipment to Japan. I still recognize that same optimism and energy in this Canada of ours, but they need sound financial encouragement if we hope to keep on building a better and more productive society.
I would now like to discuss the budget as it relates to our senior citizens. There is no doubt that they have been given reasonable consideration, but I wonder if the increase will really do much good in the area where it is most needed. I mean the area of supplying their essential drugs. I receive numerous letters from senior citizens, and drug costs are by far the biggest problem to overcome. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that if the minister could see his way clear to let these people have their prescription drug needs compensated in full, he would be supporting the class of senior citizen that is the hardest hit. There must be some way to perform this service systematically for these people. I know many who, with total drug support, could continue to live independently for much longer, and keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that these are many of the same independent individuals who built this country. They struggled and deprived themselves of what were necessities to them at that time, trusting future generations to stand by them.
The conditions today must be a bitter pill, to be forced down the throats of our senior citizens by a government that has such apparent indifference to society. "Yes," they say, "but that is all over now, that was our other face." They seem to forget the old phrase, "It's a long lane without a turn". You cannot hoodwink the people of Canada indefinitely, and a lot more than just our senior citizens will eventually prove that statement when they come to submit their 1972 tax returns.
The tax-paying public who are recipients of Canadian dividends are virtually asked to sign a return that in effect is a falsehood. It is not only a falsehood but an underhanded way to try and hoodwink these taxpayers into helping to pay for the so-called goodies in this budget, because there is a one-third levy automatically added to their T5 dividend returns which, in effect, shows them stating an income above that which they in actual fact received, even including the 20 per cent tax credit.
I know of several people who have already confronted the local tax departments on this fact, and were virtually given the opinion that it was true. Officials tried to pass it off as too complicated to explain. This puts these civil servants in an embarrassing situation, and sometimes finds them being rude to the inquiring taxpayer because remember, they are human too, and can stand only so much needling for a situation they had no part in bringing into being. So, as it now looks, there will be thousands of
25789-30j

February 23, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Frank
returns submitted unsigned, from fear of potentially falsifying these income tax statements. This government should be thoroughly exposed for such underhanded tactics.
Another area that disturbs me as a new member is the apparent lack of sincerity of some ministers in their replies to questions asked in the House. A good example is the time the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) was asked if there would be an opportunity for the citizens near Mount Hope airport to be heard. He intimated, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, we might first have the opinions of members of parliament who contend that they have been elected by the people-
This was a convenient answer, except a bit contradictory to previous positions taken by former ministers of transport. This involved pressure brought to bear on this government to extend the runways at the London airport. There were three government members at that time representing the London area, but apparently the government would not accept their advice because the mayor and a delegation, at the city's expense, had to come to Ottawa to get final approval. If we in opposition are made to feel like nobodys by this government, what of the embarrassment of those particular members, two of them being still with us?
Mr. Speaker, you have heard of honourable mentions. Well that is about all this budget gives to the farmers by eliminating the capital gains tax on family farms. That may be very credible, but if we are going to encourage young people to take over farms, capital gains tax has to be eliminated from all bona fide transactions. Statistics tells us the average age of all farmers is too high, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) tells us that an average of 12 farmers per day are leaving the industry. Mr. Speaker, that figure will get higher if they cannot afford to sell before they die.
The Minister of Agriculture has credibly increased the potential loan to a young farmer. That is fine if the farmer has any equity, but what is really needed is for the minister to encourage the balance of the provincial governments to incorporate the once-in-a-lifetime-gift for farmers, and it should include small businesses as well, to the limit of $50,000. In this way, potential family business successors, whether they be farmers or small business people, could apply to the Farm Credit Corporation or the IDB and would have a decent equity for loans, with a reasonable chance of survival.
We have a committee investigating the high cost of food. If this committee accomplishes nothing else, the least it should do is establish in the minds of urban consumers, in particular, the true role the basic producer is playing in the food production cycle. The consumer must keep in mind that the so-called cheap food policy that seems to be on so many minds today will only lead to consistently dearer foods in the future. Tariffs, basic herd and quota rights are other areas of concern in agriculture which I strongly urge the Minister of Finance to reconsider.

There are many more areas I would like to cover as this budget relates to my riding, but apparently time will not permit.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the time allotted to me this afternoon I shall try to deal with two subjects. I want to deal with some proposals of the Conservative party with respect to price and wage controls, and to talk about the importance of the manufacturing industry at a time of rapidly shifting international currents. I start with the proposal put forward yesterday by the likeable member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies.)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The party proposal.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I accept that. Your leader endorsed it today. Two weeks ago this same member, the spokesman for the economic troika of the Conservative party, stated that if the Conservatives had been elected to form a government on October 30 they would not have brought in wage and price controls. Only yesterday he said that if a Conservative government had been elected on October 30 it would have brought in wage and price controls. This is an incredible position for anyone to take and, I suggest, even more so for a Conservative. I think most would agree that the Conservatives, more than anyone, dwell in the past.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are specialists in hindsight. They are the ones who are usually looking back. But when this man looks back, he finds two stories. He has not yet made up his mind. In his speech on the budget, the hon. member for Don Valley put forward the proposal to freeze immediately all wages, prices, interest and dividends in Canada for a period of 30 to 90 days-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sixty to 90 days.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and thereafter put them under a comprehensive system of controls. Judging by the reaction this proposal had among his backbenchers and the comments of his leader today, that position has been endorsed by his party. We are aware that the Conservatives have been inching toward this position for some time. When questioned on this particular issue, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), as usual, stated, "Yes, we would not be afraid to introduce controls if necessary"- "if necessary" being underlined. Why has the Conservative party now come to the conclusion that the situation is so critical that the government should control wages and prices for Canadian workers and producers?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We heard the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When he appeared on the CBC television program "Encounter," the hon. member for Don Valley said that a move toward controls could only be made on the basis of a national emergency. I think those were his words, "a national emergency." He was asked:
Do you think that five per cent inflation would justify a national emergency?
February 23, 1973

The hon. member replied:
No, I'm not suggesting that.
Was the member really criticizing the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) for not introducing an emergency measure to deal with 5 per cent inflation? Was there any need for it at that moment?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As long as you stay over there, there is an emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Don Valley assured the viewing public, "No, no". I can understand that even if there has not developed a critical national emergency to justify the sudden conversion of the hon. member for Don Valley and other members of his party, there has at least developed a critical political emergency among Conservatives recently, one that apparently drives them to desperate last resorts. The extent of their desperation may possibly best be measured by the extent to which they have reversed their positions over the past several months.
Let me remind hon. members of some of the positions taken by leading spokesmen of the Conservative party. In a column in the Telegram, a newspaper that used to exist in Toronto and to which the hon. member for Don Valley contributed-I am not saying that had anything to do with its demise-he told his readers that he did not believe that wage and price controls were effective anti-inflationary measures.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What date?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: April, 1971.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Furthermore, he warned they would create far more problems than they might solve.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can understand the lack of interest of members opposite in being reminded of some of these remarks. He said controls were extremely difficult to administer and could only possibly be effective if they were applied to all segments of the economy and were widely accepted. In addition, he wrote:
-price and wage controls inevitably bring rationing. Once the price for a particular product is fixed, the only way it can be distributed among all the people who want it is through some such system.
It was just over two years ago-it seems like yesterday- that the government and the public were being sternly lectured by the Leader of the Opposition. I want to recall his words at that time. He complained:
There has been a lot of loose talk about wage and price controls-even cabinet ministers are mentioning it these days-as the answer to price stability in Canada.
I put these things on the record because it is obvious the Conservative party looked at these techniques and rejected them until the desperation of their political situation and frustrations caused them to reverse their position.

That was five budgets ago, Benson's three and Turner's two.
